extracted.intended_audience: general news readers interested in media, entertainment, and fact-checking disputes
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative points for judging factual claims made by comedians and for how journalists should report and fact-check those claims; illustrated by the Hasan Minhaj / New Yorker dispute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy in recounting personal experiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a comedian's retelling of events is factually accurate versus embellished or fabricated (e.g., Minhaj's prom story, meetings related to Jamal Khashoggi, claims about Jared Kushner).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article describes instances where The New Yorker said Minhaj 'elided or concocted other details in his stories, often to place himself more squarely at the center of the action.' Evaluators should check contemporaneous facts and note when performers admit to or deny inventing details; special scrutiny applies when claims concern serious matters like racism or law-enforcement encounters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different standards by format: political comedy vs. comedic storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that creators may apply different standards to different formats: political/comedic journalism aims for factual accuracy while storytelling comedy may prioritize emotional truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minhaj's own line is cited: 'In political comedy, facts come first... In comedic storytelling, emotions come first.' Use this distinction when judging whether a factual lapse is an ethical breach or a storytelling device, but weigh seriousness of subject matter (e.g., racism, police abuse) more heavily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sourcing and corroboration in journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalistic pieces should be based on careful reporting and fact-checking, with corroboration from multiple sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The New Yorker's statement: its piece 'was carefully reported and fact-checked. It is based on interviews with more than 20 people, including former Patriot Act and Daily Show staffers; members of Minhaj's security team; and people who have been the subject of his standup work.' Evaluators should look for breadth of sourcing (firsthand witnesses, staffers, documents) as evidence of a reliable report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of contemporaneous documentary evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The weight of contemporaneous records (emails, text messages, documents) in establishing what actually happened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minhaj presented 'emails and text messages' to insist he was not 'needlessly cruel' in his prom story; such documents can show timeline and tone and are persuasive counter-evidence to later recollections or accusations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admission and apology for embellishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the subject acknowledges exaggerations and apologizes when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minhaj 'says he is sorry for embellishing the story, if anyone was worrying about me and my family.' Admissions and apologies matter for public accountability and can affect judgments about intent and harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility when recounting potentially alarming incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Care with describing incidents that could cause public alarm or suggest danger (e.g., alleged anthrax/white powder incidents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minhaj clarified the white-powder envelope incident: he 'knew right away it was not anthrax' and it 'did not spill onto her and she was not rushed to the hospital.' Claims involving safety should be precise and avoid overstating danger; exaggeration here can be particularly damaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of timelines and factual details
rubrics_metrics.description: Check whether the timing and sequence of events as recounted match independent records or other witnesses (e.g., the timing of a meeting at the Saudi Embassy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The New Yorker notes a producer said a meeting referenced by Minhaj 'took place at least a month earlier.' Discrepancies in timing can indicate embellishment or faulty memory; corroboration helps resolve conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of anonymity vs. transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Balancing anonymity for individuals referenced in stories with the need for verification and context (e.g., using pseudonyms like 'Bethany' while presenting texts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minhaj calls the woman in his prom story 'Bethany' to protect her anonymity while the reporting includes quotes from unnamed sources. Evaluators should consider how anonymity is used and whether sufficient corroboration exists to support claims made about anonymous subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: How narrative framing centers the performer
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether storytellers place themselves disproportionately at the center of events, potentially altering facts to enhance personal centrality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The New Yorker accused Minhaj of adding details 'often to place himself more squarely at the center of the action.' Assess whether framing choices change the substance or implications of events and whether such choices mislead audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional and reputational consequences of factual disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition that disputes over factual accuracy can have concrete career impacts and prompt public criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes stakes such as losing consideration for The Daily Show host job and public critiques (e.g., Bill Maher's comments). Evaluators should weigh not just factual correctness but the downstream effects on trust, career opportunities, and public standing.
